query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A minor boron addition combined with a post‐processing deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) will synergistically enhance the ductility and uniform deformability of a B-doped HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory HEA while maintaining its high dynamic compressive strength and energetic energy release under high strain rate loading relative to the boron-doped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory HEA with 0.1 at.% boron (RHEA-B) as previously studied.
generation.intervention: Apply a deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) after alloy synthesis and initial boron doping.
generation.conditions: Dynamic compression at high strain rates (e.g., ~3000 s⁻¹) and ambient temperature; testing under conditions similar to energetic structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion via intergranular (Hf, Zr)B₂-type boride precipitations combined with DCT-induced compressive residual stress and potential stress‐induced phase precipitation near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron doping precipitates fine boride particles at grain boundaries to inhibit intergranular decohesion, improving ductility, whereas DCT further refines the microstructure by inducing high compressive residual stress and promoting limited stress‐induced phase transformations that can delay crack initiation. The combination is expected to retain high dynamic strength and maintain energetic reactivity by preserving a uniform microstructure that supports rapid energy release under impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a boron-doped untreated sample (baseline fracture strain ~12.3%), the combined treatment should increase the fracture strain (e.g., toward ~19% or higher) without reducing the dynamic compressive strength by more than ~10%, and with no adverse impact on energy release characteristics.
generation.baseline: Boron-doped HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory HEA (RHEA-B) as reported, which shows enhanced ductility (up to 19.3% fracture strain) but with a specific trade-off in dynamic strength and energetic performance.
generation.boundary: The improvement must hold under high strain rate dynamic conditions; if the DCT process causes excessive embrittlement or degrades the energetic reactivity (e.g., by altering the chemical reactivity or suppressing deflagration behavior), the intervention would be considered ineffective.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the ductility-enhancing effect observed from intergranular boride precipitation (PMC9572892::web::003::1_introduction, PMC9572892::web::014::3_5_macro_compressive_strength_and_ducti) by incorporating DCT-induced residual stress modification (PMC11355962::web::010::3_1_the_effect_of_cryogenic_treatment_on). What is new here is the investigation of their combined effect on dynamic mechanical performance and energy release, a gap not addressed by previous studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfMoNbTaTiZr HEA samples doped with 0.1 at.% boron. One set undergoes deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) under controlled conditions (e.g., immersion at liquid nitrogen temperatures for an optimized duration) while the control set is kept untreated post-synthesis. Subject both sets to dynamic compression tests at strain rates around 3000 s⁻¹ and perform complementary high-speed imaging and energetic reaction diagnostics.
measurements: Dynamic compressive yield strength and ultimate strength
Energy release characteristics (e.g., reaction delay time, intensity of deflagration) using high-speed cameras and pressure sensors
Microstructural analysis (grain-boundary integrity, residual stress via XRD, and phase characterization via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DCT-treated, boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in fracture strain (e.g., <10% improvement over the control) or if the dynamic compressive strength or energetic reaction parameters fall outside acceptable bounds (i.e., strength decreased by more than 10% or energy release is substantially diminished) compared to the untreated RHEA-B, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. The Effect of Cryogenic Treatment on Residual Stress of the Alloy
cited_evidence.text: In view of the influence of residual stress on grain structure, it is considered that a sharp decrease in alloy temperature causes the grain to shrink, which constructs the tensile stress state between grains, assisted by the mutual restraint of the grains (Figure 4A,B). In the process from B to C, the line defects inside the grains are generated under the action of continuous tensile stress and expand with the increase in soaking time. The accompanying plastic deformation partially relaxes the tensile thermal stress. When the soaking time increases to a certain extent, the tensile stress between the crystals promotes stress-induced phase transition. Then, as the HEA sample is reheated back to room temperature at the end of the DCT process (states C to D), due to the crystalline defects and plastic deformation, as well as the intergranular constraints, a state of compressive residual stress remains in the particles. In order to provide a further basis for this hypothesis, the finite element simulation (FE simulation) method based on ABAQUS software was used to simulate the internal stress of the alloy during LMD and DCT processes.

Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

The minor addition of boron effectively improved the mechanical properties of the alloy, as presented in the macro-compressive stress–strain curves and fractographies of the RHEA and RHEA-B samples in Figure 7, and as the yield stresses, ultimate strengths, fracture strains and work hardening percentages listed in Table 4. While the yield stress only slightly increased from 1.57 GPa for the RHEA (close to the value obtained by the above micropillar compression, 1.51 GPa) to 1.61 GPa for the RHEA-B, the work hardenability and ductility were more obviously improved. The ultimate compressive strength of the RHEA, 1.75 GPa at a fracture stain of 12.3%, showed a similarly low hardenability (for only about 11%) and ductility to typical refractory alloys. In comparison, The RHEA-B exhibited a much higher ultimate compressive strength of 2.05 GPa (hardening for 27%) and fracture stain up to 19.3%. The compressive-engineering-stress-versus-engineering-strain curves of the Ce5 at strain rates ranging from 10−3 s−1 to 5000 s−1 are shown in Figure 5a. Under quasi-static compression, the yield strength, compressive ultimate strength and fracture strain were 1000 MPa, 1367 MPa and 23%, respectively. At the beginning of loading, the alloy showed linear elastic characteristics. With the increase in strain, the resistance to deformation continued to increase and the material underwent work hardening. In this stage, internal micropores and microcracks accumulated along the grain boundaries. After reaching the highest compressive strength, the stress began to fall until the specimen fractured, at which point it was essentially the growth and aggregation of defects within the material. Under dynamic compression, the yield stage was not obvious. Instead, it was slowly unloaded in the form of strain softening after the stress reached the highest compressive strength, indicating a reduction in material plasticity.
